questions.q: What is server-side template injection (SSTI)?
choices: When an attacker injects native template syntax into a template that is then executed server-side
When an attacker overwrites static files served by the template engine
When a template is rendered in the victim's browser using attacker-supplied JavaScript
When a template engine leaks its source code over an unencrypted channel
questions.explain: SSTI occurs when an attacker is able to use native template syntax to inject a malicious payload into a template, which is then executed server-side.

questions.q: Server-side template injection payloads are delivered and evaluated client-side, in the victim's browser.
questions.explain: SSTI payloads are delivered and evaluated server-side, which potentially makes them much more dangerous than typical client-side template injection.

questions.q: Template engines generate web pages by combining fixed templates with volatile ______ (fill in the blank).
questions.explain: Template engines combine fixed templates with volatile data. SSTI arises when user input is treated as part of the template itself rather than as data.

questions.q: Why can SSTI be more dangerous than a typical client-side template injection?
choices: Because the payload is evaluated server-side, potentially giving control of the back-end server
Because browsers cannot filter template syntax
Because it only affects logic-less template engines
Because it always bypasses TLS encryption
questions.explain: As the name suggests, SSTI payloads are evaluated server-side, potentially making them much more dangerous than client-side template injection.

questions.q: At the most severe end of the scale, what can an attacker achieve through SSTI?
choices: Remote code execution and full control of the back-end server
Only a denial-of-service crash of the template engine
Nothing beyond a cosmetic change to a rendered page
questions.explain: At the severe end, an attacker can potentially achieve remote code execution, taking full control of the back-end server and using it to attack internal infrastructure.

questions.q: Even when full remote code execution is not possible, SSTI can still be used as the basis for other attacks such as reading sensitive data and arbitrary files.
questions.explain: Even without RCE, an attacker can often use SSTI to gain read access to sensitive data and arbitrary files on the server.

questions.q: According to the material, how often do SSTI vulnerabilities pose no real security risk?
choices: In roughly half of all cases
questions.explain: In certain rare circumstances SSTI poses no real security risk, but most of the time the impact can be catastrophic.

questions.q: SSTI vulnerabilities arise when user input is handled in what way?
choices: Concatenated directly into templates rather than passed in as data
Passed into templates strictly as data via placeholders
Stored in a database before rendering
questions.explain: SSTI arises when user input is concatenated into templates rather than being passed in as data.

questions.q: Static templates that simply provide placeholders into which dynamic content is rendered are generally vulnerable to SSTI.
questions.explain: Static templates that use placeholders for dynamic content are generally NOT vulnerable, because user input is passed in as data rather than becoming part of the template.

questions.q: Which Twig example is vulnerable to SSTI?
choices: A template that stores the name in a session variable
A template that logs the name to a file
questions.explain: Concatenating the GET parameter into the template string (`render("Dear " . $_GET['name'])`) makes part of the template itself user-controlled. Passing first_name in as array data is safe.

questions.q: The material compares accidental SSTI (from concatenating user input into templates) to which classic injection flaw found in poorly written prepared statements?
questions.explain: It is described as similar to SQL injection vulnerabilities occurring in poorly written prepared statements.

questions.q: Which is given as an example of SSTI being introduced intentionally rather than by accident?
choices: Deliberately allowing privileged users such as content editors to edit or submit custom templates
Using a logic-less template engine by default
Running templates inside a Docker container
questions.explain: Some websites deliberately allow privileged users (e.g., content editors) to edit or submit custom templates by design, which is a huge risk if such an account is compromised.

questions.q: What sequence of special characters does the material suggest injecting to fuzz a template for SSTI?
questions.explain: Fuzzing with the sequence ${{<%[%'"}}%\ and watching for a raised exception is a simple first approach — an error suggests the injected template syntax is being interpreted.

questions.q: SSTI occurs in two distinct contexts, each requiring its own detection method. What are they?
questions.explain: SSTI occurs in a plaintext context and a code context, each of which requires its own detection approach.

questions.q: SSTI in the plaintext context can sometimes be exploited for XSS and is in fact often mistaken for a simple XSS vulnerability.
questions.explain: In the plaintext context, freely input content rendered to HTML can be exploited for XSS and is often mistaken for plain XSS — testing with a math operation helps reveal the SSTI.

questions.q: If injecting username=${7*7} into a vulnerable plaintext-context template outputs "Hello 49", the math was evaluated server-side. What numeric value appears?
questions.explain: Output of "Hello 49" shows the mathematical operation ${7*7} was evaluated server-side — a good proof of concept for SSTI.

questions.q: In the code context, after confirming there is no direct XSS, what is the next step to test for SSTI?
choices: Try to break out of the statement using template syntax, e.g. injecting }}<tag>, and see if arbitrary HTML renders
Submit the same value repeatedly to cause a timeout
Replace the whole parameter with a base64 blob
Request the page over HTTP instead of HTTPS
questions.explain: After ruling out direct XSS, you try to break out of the statement with common templating syntax (e.g. greeting=data.username}}<tag>). Correctly rendered output plus the arbitrary HTML indicates SSTI.

questions.q: What is often the simplest way to identify which template engine is in use?
choices: Submit invalid syntax so the resulting error message reveals the engine (and sometimes the version)
Read the HTTP Server response header
Count the number of rendered HTML tags
questions.explain: Submitting invalid syntax is often enough, because the error message will tell you exactly which template engine (and sometimes which version) is being used.

questions.q: The invalid expression <%=foobar%> triggers an "undefined local variable or method" error. Which template engine does this identify?
questions.explain: <%=foobar%> triggers a NameError from the Ruby-based ERB engine, identifying it.

questions.q: The payload {{7*'7'}} returns 49 in Twig. What does it return in Jinja2?
questions.explain: {{7*'7'}} returns 49 in Twig and 7777777 in Jinja2, showing why you shouldn't jump to conclusions from a single response.

questions.q: The same payload can sometimes return a successful response in more than one template language, so you should not conclude the engine from a single successful response.
questions.explain: For example {{7*'7'}} succeeds in both Twig (49) and Jinja2 (7777777); it is important not to jump to conclusions based on a single successful response.

questions.q: When error messages don't reveal the engine, what manual technique helps narrow down the template language?
choices: Injecting arbitrary math operations in different engines' syntax and observing which are evaluated, using a process of elimination
Measuring the page's response time for each request
questions.explain: You manually test language-specific payloads — commonly arbitrary math operations in each engine's syntax — and use a process of elimination (aided by a decision tree) to narrow the options.

questions.q: Select the activities that make up the "Read" phase of exploiting SSTI.
choices: Look for known, documented exploits online
Deploy the template inside a Docker container
Run a port scan of the back-end server
questions.explain: The Read phase covers learning the basic template syntax, reading the documentation's security section/warnings, and looking for known exploits. Docker and port scanning are not part of it.

questions.q: The Mako template engine — where RCE can be as simple as an <% import os %> block calling os.popen('id') — is based on which language?
questions.explain: Mako is a Python-based template engine; knowing how to embed native code blocks can quickly lead to RCE in an unsandboxed environment.

questions.q: In the Java-based Velocity engine, the exploit $class.inspect("java.lang.Runtime").type.getRuntime().exec(...) works by chaining which members of the ClassTool object?
questions.explain: In Velocity, chaining the $class.inspect() method and $class.type property yields references to arbitrary objects — used here to reach Runtime and execute shell commands.

questions.q: In Java-based templating languages, what injection does the material give for listing all environment variables (to help enumerate objects in scope)?
questions.explain: ${T(java.lang.System).getenv()} lists environment variables, helping build a shortlist of interesting objects and methods to investigate.

questions.q: If remote code execution has been ruled out (for example in a sandboxed engine), there is no remaining potential for any SSTI exploit.
questions.explain: Ruling out RCE doesn't rule out other high-severity exploits — e.g., file path traversal to access sensitive data, often via developer-supplied objects.

questions.q: Why should you pay particular attention to developer-supplied (site-specific) objects rather than only built-in objects?
choices: They are especially likely to contain sensitive information or exploitable methods and form a less battle-hardened attack surface
They are always documented in detail by the template engine
They cannot be reached from within a template
They are automatically sandboxed and therefore safe
questions.explain: Non-standard developer-supplied objects are especially likely to hold sensitive data or exploitable methods, and (unlike built-ins) are almost never documented, offering a less battle-hardened attack surface.

questions.q: What is described as the best way to prevent SSTI?
choices: Do not allow any users to modify or submit new templates
Use a longer secret key for the template engine
questions.explain: The best prevention is to not allow users to modify or submit new templates — though business requirements sometimes make this unavoidable.

questions.q: Which "logic-less" template engine is given as an example that reduces exposure to the most dangerous template-based attacks?
questions.explain: Using a logic-less template engine such as Mustache separates logic from presentation and greatly reduces exposure to the most dangerous template-based attacks.

questions.q: Sandboxing untrusted template code is a reliable, foolproof defense against SSTI.
questions.explain: Sandboxing untrusted code is inherently difficult and prone to bypasses; it is only one measure and not foolproof.

questions.q: As a complementary defense that accepts code execution may be inevitable, the material suggests deploying the template environment inside what?
questions.explain: A complementary approach is to accept that arbitrary code execution may be inevitable and apply your own sandboxing, e.g., by deploying the template environment in a locked-down Docker container.
